# HELP WANTED: Scientists Seeking Senior Dogs To Unlock the Secrets of Aging

Image: Dr. Paola Cuevas

By Dr. Paola CuevasUpdated on October 20, 2026

Share

Ask us a question in the comments

Image: HELP WANTED: Scientists Seeking Senior Dogs To Unlock the Secrets of Aging

What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

That is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is currently looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

* * *

### Why Rapamycin?

Rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

The interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

The Dog Aging Project’s TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

Image

### It’s Not Just About Lifespan

For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

Lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

Those are not the same thing.

# Feline small cell GI lymphoma: A cancer that overlaps with IBD

Author(s)Abi Bautista-Alejandre, Assistant Editor

Fact checked by: Yasmeen Qahwash

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) may progress to feline small cell gastrointestinal (GI) lymphoma, researchers say. Texas A&M University is testing a new treatment option for the cancer.

Developing slowly over months to years, feline small cell gastrointestinal (GI) lymphoma can be difficult to detect.^{1} With this type of cancer resembling many of the common digestive issues cats often experience, understanding the disease, warning signs, diagnosis, and treatment is important to ensure the well-being of feline patients with chronic GI symptoms.

GI lymphoma in cats is divided between small cell and large cell. Unlike small cell lymphoma, signs for large cell lymphoma develop quickly, over days to weeks, and the prognosis is poorer.^{2}

According to the North Carolina State Veterinary Hospital, cats with large cell GI lymphoma receiving CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone) therapy have a prognosis of 6 to 9 months.^{2} Meanwhile, cats with small cell GI lymphoma have a longer prognosis of typically 2 to 3 years or more, but chronic treatment with oral medications is required.^{2}

## The ins and outs of small cell GI lymphoma

Small cell GI lymphoma forms in the digestive tract. Affecting lymphocytes (immune cells involved in fighting off infection), lymphoma causes uncontrolled cell growth and loss of normal cell function. According to Texas A&M University, the GI tract is home to a high number of lymphocytes, making it a common site of lymphoma in feline patients.^{1} In fact, small cell GI lymphoma is the most common type of lymphoma in cats^{3} and is the most frequently diagnosed digestive tract cancer in these animals.^{1}

“Small cell GI lymphoma is the most common cancer of a cat’s digestive system and a highly prevalent feline cancer overall,” Regina Hayburn, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), a clinical assistant professor of medical oncology at Texas A&M’s Department of Small Animal Clinical Sciences, said in the Texas A&M report.^{1} “It can form anywhere along the digestive tract, including the stomach, small intestine, or colon.”

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and small cell GI lymphoma are thought to be closely related, representing different stages of the same underlying process. Veterinary researchers have found that GI inflammatory lesions, a major characteristic of IBD, often coexist with small cell GI lymphoma.^{4} This overlap has led to the proposition that chronic inflammatory lesions might progress to lymphoma over time.^{4} As such, many researchers and veterinarians have described small cell GI lymphoma as being a “spectrum of disease” with IBD.^{1,4}

“Because of the impaired motility and absorption, chronic vomiting and diarrhea are common, along with weight loss and decreased appetite, although some cats maintain a normal or even increased appetite in early stages,” Hayburn said in the Texas A&M report.^{1} “As the disease progresses, cats often stop eating, vomit more frequently, and become increasingly lethargic and generally unwell due to chronic illness and weight loss.” Bloody stools may also be a sign of small cell GI lymphoma and IBD.

【turn985search1】 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Aug 28, 2026 — Explanations about what cancer is, how cancer cells differ from normal cells, and genetic changes that cause cancer to grow and spread.
  * grow in the absence of signals telling them to grow. Normal cells only grow when they receive such signals.
  * ignore signals that normally tell cells to stop dividing or to die (a process known as programmed cell death, or apoptosis).
  * invade into nearby areas and spread to other areas of the body. Normal cells stop growing when they encounter other cells, and most normal cells do not move around the body.
Many times, cancer cells rely so heavily on these abnormal behaviors that they can’t survive without them. Researchers have taken advantage of this fact, developing therapies that target the abnormal features of cancer cells. For example, some cancer therapies prevent blood vessels from growing toward tumors, essentially starving the tumor of needed nutrients.  

Image

Cancer is a disease caused when cells divide uncontrollably and spread into surrounding tissues.

Enlarge Image

## 

How Does Cancer Develop?

Cancer is a genetic disease—that is, it is caused by changes to genes that control the way our cells function, especially how they grow and divide.

Genetic changes that cause cancer can happen because:

The body normally eliminates cells with damaged DNA before they turn cancerous. But the body’s ability to do so goes down as we age. This is part of the reason why there is a higher risk of cancer later in life.

Each person’s cancer has a unique combination of genetic changes. As the cancer continues to grow, additional changes will occur. Even within the same tumor, different cells may have different genetic changes.

Genetic changes that cause cancer can be inherited or arise from certain environmental exposures. Genetic changes can also happen because of errors that occur as cells divide.

Credit: National Cancer Institute

Enlarge Image

Image

Most often, cancer-causing genetic changes accumulate slowly as a person ages, leading to a higher risk of cancer later in life.

Enlarge Image

## 

Types of Genes that Cause Cancer

Image

A DNA change can cause genes involved in normal cell growth to become oncogenes. Unlike normal genes, oncogenes cannot be turned off, so they cause uncontrolled cell growth.

Enlarge Image

The genetic changes that contribute to cancer tend to affect three main types of genes—proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and DNA repair genes. These changes are sometimes called “drivers” of cancer.

Title: Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome with a Dual-LLM Consensus Pipeline
Authors: Daniel Palacios, Guantong Qi, Mikael Guzman Karlsson, Shawntel K. David, Mohammed Sameeruddin, Bernhard Suter, Zhandong Liu, Davut Pehlivan, Hu Chen
Date: Thu Oct 15 15:24:47 2026

Objective: Trofinetide, approved in 2023 as the first Rett syndrome treatment, lacks scalable real-world monitoring because chart review is labor-intensive. We developed a dual large language model (LLM) consensus pipeline to extract 18 treatment-response phenotypes, comprising 4 adverse effects, 13 Rett clinical features, and medication refusal, from clinical notes. Materials and Methods: We analyzed 26,763 notes from 108 patients with confirmed sustained trofinetide exposure at Texas Children's Hospital. The pipeline filters notes by keyword, classifies each through two LLMs requiring consensus, and aggregates a patient-by-timepoint matrix. Architecture and prompt were selected on a diarrhea development set, then frozen and applied to the other 17 phenotypes with the phenotype definition substituted, as an out-of-sample test.
